entry.title: Teaching dimension, VC dimension, and critical sets in Latin squares
entry.summary: A critical set in an $n \times n$ Latin square is a minimal set of entries that uniquely identifies it among all Latin squares of the same size. It is conjectured by Nelder in 1979, and later independently by Mahmoodian, and Bate and van Rees that the size of the smallest critical set is $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$. We prove a lower-bound of $n^2/10^4$ for sufficiently large $n$, and thus confirm the quadratic order predicted by the conjecture. We prove a lower-bound of $n^2/10^4$ for sufficiently large $n$, and thus confirm the quadratic order predicted by the conjecture. This improves a recent lower-bound of $Ω(n^{3/2})$ due to Cavenagh and Ramadurai. From the point of view of computational learning theory, the size of the smallest critical set corresponds to the minimum teaching dimension of the set of Latin squares. We study two related notions of dimension from learning theory. We prove a lower-bound of $n^2-(e+o(1))n^{5/3}$ for both of the VC-dimension and the recursive teaching dimension.

entry.title: A counting proof for the smallest critical set in a Latin square
entry.summary: A critical set in a Latin square is a set of entries that determines the square uniquely and is minimal with this property. We prove that every partial Latin square of order $n$ with fewer than $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ filled cells has an even number of completions. Consequently every critical set in every Latin square of order $n$ has at least $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ entries. Since the cyclic Latin square has a critical set of exactly this size, the minimum size of a critical set over all Latin squares of order $n$ is $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$. This confirms a conjecture attributed to Nelder (1979) and made independently by Mahmoodian and by Bate and van Rees. Hatami and Qian had shown that this minimum is at least $n^2/10^4$ for large $n$. The proof is a counting argument modulo two that uses only expansion of products, cancellation in pairs and the pigeonhole principle, and it is illustrated with partial Latin squares of orders three to seven. An appendix discloses the substantial use of AI in developing the proof and writing the exposition.

entry.title: On the size of the minimum critical set of a Latin square
entry.summary: A critical set in an $n \times n$ array is a set $C$ of given entries, such that there exists a unique extension of $C$ to an $n\times n$ Latin square and no proper subset of $C$ has this property. For a Latin square $L$, $\scs{L}$ denotes the size of the smallest critical set of $L$, and $\scs{n}$ is the minimum of $\scs{L}$ over all Latin squares $L$ of order $n$. We find an upper bound for the number of partial Latin squares of size $k$ and prove that $$n^2-(e+o(1))n^{10/6} \le \max \scs{L} \le n^2-\frac{\sqrtπ}{2}n^{9/6}.$$ % This improves a result of N. Cavenagh (Ph.D. thesis, The University of Queensland, 2003) and disproves one of his conjectures. Also it improves the previously known lower bound for the size of the largest critical set of any Latin square of order $n$.
